Sixty-Sixth Annual Report 


Year ending April 30th, 1917 


The Young Men’s Christian Association 
of the City of Montreal 


The 


Young Men’s Christian Association 


of the City of Montreal 


Organized 185] Incorporated 1872 


BRANCHES OF THE ASSOCIATION: 


DRUMMOND ST:—127 Drummond Street 


NORTH —Park Avenue and St. Viateur 
WESTMOUNT  —Sherbrooke and ‘Arlington 
RAILROAD —Leber and Sebastopol, Point St. Charles 
EAST END —COMMUNITY 
STUDENT ASSOCIATION—McGill University 
(In Affiliation) 


General Office of 
THE BOARD OF DIRECTORS 
127 Drummond Street, 


Montreal 


OUR Directors have pleasure in presenting this, the 
Sixty-Sixth Annual Report of the Association. and in so 
doing, wish to express their gratitude for the many 

blessings of the year and for the good friends whose co-operation 
has so largely made possible the results secured. 


In these days of the great world war, the helpful ministry 
of the Association has become world wide. In the most varied 
and practical ways our Secretaries and workers are co-operating 
with the Army and Navy, munition workers, the various ex. 
peditionary forces both at home and abroad. in the training 
camps, at the firing line and wherever the tide of war has carried 
our young men in thisyvast conflict. Thousands of helpers have 
been raised up from the different walks in life to assist in this 
large enterprise. Leading ministers and professors in Great 
Britain especially are active in these ministrations, leaving their 
pulpits and chairs for months at a time. The war work of the 
Association is thus proving a great field for practical Christian 
service, co-operation and unity. 


The conviction grows upon us that the Association is one 
of the greatest assets of the Christian Church to-day. As a 
great lay brotherhood, it is carrying the essential message of 
the Church, expressing in word and deed the ministry of Christ 
and developing leadership through activity in new channels 
which will surely be of great service to the Church in the days 
of reconstruction to follow. 


The entry of the United States into the war has further 
enlarged the opportunity of the Association to serve the soldier. 
Plans have been matured by the International Committee to 
provide a force of at least 1,000 Secretaries, and a Fund of 
$3,000,000.00 is now being raised to establish work at at least 
200 points in America. The ministry, on behalf of war prisoners 
in the Allied and enemy countries of Europe, will be maintained 
so far as possible through workers from the few remaining 
neutral nations, and the financial support which has come from 
America will be continued. 

Our own Canadian Y.M.C.A. war work both at home and 
overseas has greatly enlarged during the year, until now over 
80 Secretaries are rendering service to our men in England and 
France under the wise, capable and devoted leadership of Major 
Birks. We feel sure his hands have been strengthened by the 


1 


co-operation of Mr. Kingman, Mr. Budge and Mr. Corbett at 
the London office. It has been a great satisfaction to the Board 
to have Mr. Budge, our veteran Secretary, free to co-operate 
at the Headquarters in London during this great development 
of our Canadian Association work. Major Birks is now in this 
Country and will soon return to Montreal to lay before the 
members of the Association, and our citizens generally, the 
needs of the Military Service Fund. 


The Branches. The activities of the Association largely 
find expression in the work of our several Branches, whose 
Reports in detail have been recently presented at their Annual 
Meetings, so that it is only necessary in this report to mention 
certain outstanding features. 


The three new Buildings have now been occupied by the 
Central, Westmount and North Branches for five years and are 
giving good service. Various minor alterations have been made 
during the past year, which add to the convenience of operation! 
At the North Branch, a re-arrangement of the Offices, Lobby 
and entrance to the Gymnasium and Locker Room has been 
an improvement. At the Westmount Branch, similar improve- 
ments have been made in the rooms for the Boys’ Work, pro- 
vided for largely by the generosity of a number of members. 
Filtration plants for the swimming pools have been installed 
at each of the three City Branches. The cost of these instal- 
lations is being divided over a term of years. 


All the Branches have administered their affairs with the 
utmost regard for economy and have felt the absence of so many 
members at the front. The feeling of unrest due to the war has 
had a restraining effect upon activities and made impossible 
many features which in normal times would have been under- 
taken. 

Special mention should be made of the large use of the 
Central Building on Sunday afternoon by the soldiers in train- 
ing in the City, particularly those from a distance who remained 
in the City for longer or shorter periods. The Song Service and 
Meeting in the afternoon, followed by the social Tea, has meant 
a great deal to these men away from home. It is interesting, 
also, to note that the Dormitories at Central, with accommo- 
dation for 180 men, took care of 1,384 men during the year, 
showing the changing character of work amongst young men. 
We find also, that owing to the war, the average age of men 
rooming in the Building has increased from 22 years to 29 years. 


At the Railroad Branch, Point St. Charles, we were re- 
quired to install fire protection equipment and fire escape, 
which added to the expense of operation at this point. Special 


2 


emphasis was laid upon the work for boys there this year with 
good results. 

At the request of the Officials of the Grand Trunk Railway, 
we co-operated with the Company in re-opening the small 
building at Southwark, near St. Lambert, for the benefit of the’ 
trainmen running in to the Southwark yards. Owing to the 
peculiar conditions surrounding the work at that point, a formal 
organization has not yet been developed and the work is being 
carried on under a special agreement with the Railroad Company 
until the issue is more clearly determined. 


Since the Fall of 1913, active work has been carried on at 
the East End Branch, making use of rented rooms, first at 1333 
Papineau Avenue and subsequently at 806 Papineau Avenue. 
Last year it was agreed to follow what is known as the Com- 
munity Programme, by which the rented rooms became the 
headquarters for Committee meetings and such activities as 
could be held there; other features being promoted at the 
William Dawson School and in the Churches. Your Board 
agreed to contribute dollar for dollar towards the rent and local 
expenses in addition to the services of the Secretary, Mr. 
Bradford, our Community Secretary, giving half of his time. 
In January last, the work was again specially considered and it 
was found that the members of the Board of Management were 
unwilling to continue in rented rooms, unless the Association 
could make some definite promise concerning a Branch Building 
in the near future. Owing to the war, the Board found itself 
unable to make such a promise and it was, therefore, decided to 
discontinue the Branch form of organization but to continue 
the activities on the Community basis with the needs of the 
older boy especially in mind. 


The rented rooms were relinquished on May 1st and the 
Branch organization discontinued. In the Fall, an office will be 
secured as headquarters and the work continued on the Com- 
munity basis, several of the members of the former Board of 
Management serving as a Committee. 


The experience of the last three years shows that there is 
a definite field and need for work in the East End such as the 
Association can do, but it is not yet clear that there is the finan- 
cial support in membership or subscriptions necessary to success. 
The view is held that the provision of a properly equipped 
Building would reveal sufficient interest, but our experience of 
the last three years does not enable us to verify this view. There 
is no doubt that the absence of so many young men at the war 
has greatly affected this section of the City, as all others, but 
the point which is here in doubt will have to be carefully 


3 


considered when the war is over and it is possible to resume 
the expansion of the work and the erection of Branch Buildings. 


The total membership of the Association shows a decrease 
of 977 as compared with last year, largely owing to the absence 
of any special membership campaign this year.

The Community Committee. One half of Mr. Bradford's 
time has been given to the East End Branch. Two Playgrounds . 
and a Daily Vacation Bible School were promoted during the 
summer months, followed by gymnasium classes and social 
evenings at the William Dawson School during the fall and 
winter months. 


The rooms of the Branch were used as headquarters for 
lectures, educational classes, boys’ groups, Committee meetings, 
etc. Practical co-operation was given several of the Churches 
in the introduction of the Canadian Standard Efficiency Tests 
for work amongst the boys. 


The general programme of the Community Committee has 
been directed by Mr. Bradford at other points in the City, 
particularly in connection with the Public and High Schools. 
A great deal of this work has been educational in reference to 
boy life and its needs. Lectures and talks were arranged for 
the older boys on Citizenship, Education, Life Problems, etc. 

At the request of the Faculty of the Theological Colleges, 
a series of lectures on Social Service were given by Mr. Bradford 
during the winter term, the same forming part of the regular 
curriculum. Lines of investigation have been followed and a 
great deal of thought and study given to the need for the ex- 
tension of the activities of the Association in various parts of the 
City, all of which will doubtless bear fruit in due time. 

Much time has been given to co-operation with other or- 
ganizations interested in boy life. 

Military. The work for soldiers outside of the Association 
Buildings has been continued effectively during the year under 
the direction of the Military Committee. Last Spring, in view 
of the number of units in process of organization in the City and 


4 


of the number of returned soldiers, it was felt that we needed 
the services of a capable worker for the entire twelve months of 
the year. Arrangements were then made with the National 
Council, whereby the services of Mr. John S. Gibb were secured, 
Mr. Gibb entering upon his duties in August, 1916. 


Until quite recently, the Recreation Room at the Guy 
Street Barracks has been the principal centre of activity. En- 
tertainments of various kinds have been given there; Sunday 
evening Song Services conducted; games, reading and writing 
material and other attractions provided for the troops. 


In addition, Mr. Gibb has visited the other units throughout 
the City, also the Convalescent Homes, Hospitals, etc., wherever 
he could be of service. 


Special thought and attention has been given to the needs 
of returning soldiers and to after-the-war-conditions. There is 
no question that large opportunities will present themselves for 
usefulness at the close of the war and these are receiving the 
earnest consideration of the Military Committee. 


Summer Camps. Montreal is most fortunate in being 
within easy reach of one of the most attractive recreation areas 
in the world—the Laurentian Mountains—and our Association 
is equally fortunate in being the possessor of two beautiful 
camping locations where the men and the boys may find vaca- 
tion opportunities that are unique. 


Each season our Secretaries return from the Camps pro- 
foundly impressed with their value as a means of getting better 
acquainted with the members and of coming into helpful 
personal relation with them growing out of the informal and 
delightful intimacies of the simple life there amongst the hills. 


The Men's Camp was open last season from July 14th to 
August 19th with a total attendance of 131—from the Central 
Branch 92, North Branch 26, Railroad 8, Westmount 4, McGill 
1. Mr. Henderson had charge during the two weeks in July, 
followed by Mr. MacLaren for one week, and Mr. Holliday for 
the last two weeks. Various minor improvements were made 
to the property and a very helpful season spent. A credit 
balance of $40.60 remained. 


The Boys’ Camp opened on June 24th, continuing until 
August 18th. The attendance reached 175, as follows —Central 
Branch 68, Westmount Branch 54, North Branch 53. 

Mr. MacKinnon acted as Leader throughout, assisted by a 
splendid group of volunteers. Various improvements were 
made in the equipment and a credit balance of $217.18 remained. 
A site for a new baseball field near the Camp has been located 


5 


through the kindness of Mr. W. D. Staveley, C.E., and its pur- 
chase authorized. The educational and religious features of the 
life of our Boys’ Camp are now well understood, and of the 
greatest value in the life of the boy. Our friends can do no 
better thing for their boys than to give them a season at 
Kanawana. 

Current Finances. The Treasurer's Statement, which will 
be laid before you this evening, will reveal gratifying activity 
on the part of the Finance Committee. The total amount re- 
ceived in subscriptions through the Joint Fund this year has 
been $21,842.10, as compared with $10,341.50 the previous 
year. This has enabled the Committee to appropriate to the 
Branches the sum of $9,648.59, as compared with $2,746.00, a 
year ago. The principal reason for this increase in subscriptions 
has been the necessity for alterations and equipment in our 
Branch Buildings, most of which had been deferred at the out- 
break of war but which had become an absolute necessity to, 
the conduct of activities. 

This increase was largely provided for through a special 
canvass for new subscriptions undertaken on October 17-18-19 
last, when nearly $4,000.00 was secured from new sources in 
three days.

The Board have been impressed with the importance of 
creating an Endowment Fund, the income from same to be 
applied to the Budget of the Metropolitan Board, but until 
other obligations are discharged, the Board have felt it would be 
impossible to do this unless legacies were received under this 
condition. . 

As the work of the Association enlarges in the City, the 
importance of such a Fund increases, and your Directors would 
respectfully call the attention of friends of the Association to 
the propriety of thus strengthening the work for the future. 

Property. The Building Fund Note which last year 
amounted to $18,734.41 has been reduced to $16,000.00, the 
following amounts having been applied to its reduction during 


the year: 
Balance of Orkney Fund...............+..%. $ 690.00

$2,734.41 


Consideration was given to the sale of the vacant lots now 
held on Wellington Street for the Point St. Charles Branch, and 
Papineau Avenue lot for the East End Branch, and after con- 
ference with the respective Boards of Management it was de- 
cided to retain the Wellington Street lots for the present but to 
endeavor to sell the Papineau Avenue lot. So far, no sale has 
been effected. 


The mortgage on the Central, Westmount and North 
Branch Buildings held by the Law Union & Rock Insurance 
Company, amounting to $60,000.00, becomes due on December 
31st next. It is the recommendation of your Directors that this 
mortgage be renewed and also enlarged to $70,000.00, so as to 
reduce the Building Fund Note of $16,000.00 by the amount of 
$10,000.00, and an offer has been received from the above Com- 
pany and accepted by the Board for such renewal and enlarge- 
ment at a rate of 6% interest for a further period of three or five 
years. This matter will be placed before you at the special 
meeting this evening. 


The first mortgage on the Papineau Avenue lot of $7,000.00 
fell due on March 25th last and in view of the proposed reduc- 
tion of the Building Fund Note a second Note was arranged at 
the Merchants Bank of $7,000.00 and this mortgage retired. 
When the new arrangements concerning the mortgage on the 
Buildings are completed on December 31st next, we will combine 
the balance of the Building Fund Note amounting to $6,000.00 
with this loan of $7,000.00, making an obligation to the Bank of 
$13,000.00 in all, subject to previous reduction, should the 
opportunity arise. 

The second mortgage on the Papineau Avenue lot amount- 
ing to $7,000.00 fell due on June 7th, and was reduced by a 
payment of $2,000.00 from Legacy Account. The balance of 
$5,000.00 to continue for a further term of three years at 6%. 


The mortgage on the Point St. Charles lots was renewed 
for three years at 6%. 

Honor Roll. We remember gratefully to-night, those of our 
number now at the front whose names appear on the Honor Roll 
at our several Branches and whose services with those of all our 
Canadian men overseas, will never be forgotten. We would fain 
pay our tribute of respect to those who have fallen and we trust 
the memory of their courage and self-sacrifice will be an inspira- 
tion to us in the path of duty. 

Staff Changes—Central. N. W. Parker resigned in De- 
cember to take charge of the Railroad work at Southwark and 
was succeeded by Mr. Spence. Dr. G. A. Smith was granted 
leave of absence for Army Medical Work overseas. Mr. M. F. 


ff 


Furey, recently Physical Director at Lowell, Mass., has taken 
charge of the Physical Work at Central, commencing May 1st. 


Westmount. Mr. R. W. Young, of the Springfield College, 
became Physical Director at Westmount in September. Mr. E. 
Hobson, Boys’ Work Secretary, resigned in August, and was 
succeeded by Mr. E. M. Crawford. 

North. Mr. A. L. Walsh, Boys’ Work Secretary, resigned 
to enter College and was succeeded by Mr. S. B. Cuthbert. 

Railroad. Mr. C. H. Folmsbee succeeded Mr. Johnston as 
Physical Director. Mr. J. R. Mercer, Secretary, resigned March 
15th to take the Secretaryship at Kenora, and has been suc- 
ceeded by Mr. J. R. Dalley. 

In October last, our General Secretary was honored by 
receiving a call from the International Committee to join their 
Staff as Senior Secretary of the City Association Department, 
and to the regret of the Directors, has accepted this call. By 
the courtesy of the International Committee, he has been: 
enabled to continue his connection with this Association for 
the present, spending about one-third of his time in New York 
at his new duties. 

We regret to record the death of the following subscribers 
during the year 1916-17.
